steps: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that enables machines to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning and problem-solving.
The idea of intelligent machines developed over many years, alongside advances in mathematics, logic and computing.
In 1950, Alan Turing proposed a test for considering whether a machine could show intelligent behaviour; it later became known as the Turing Test.
In 1956, the term “Artificial Intelligence” was introduced at the Dartmouth conference, which is often regarded as the beginning of AI as a formal field of study.
Early AI programs focused on solving logical problems and playing games. Limited computer power and high expectations led to periods of slower progress, sometimes called AI winters.
From the 1980s, expert systems used rules and knowledge supplied by specialists to help make decisions in particular fields.
With larger datasets and more powerful computers, machine learning enabled computers to learn patterns from data rather than relying only on fixed rules.
In the 2010s, deep learning and neural networks made major advances in areas such as image recognition, speech recognition and language processing.

Today, AI is used in applications such as virtual assistants, recommendation systems, translation, healthcare and self-driving technology; generative AI can also create text, images and other content.
AI has therefore evolved from rule-based problem-solving programs to data-driven learning systems that can perform increasingly complex tasks.
items.finalAnswer: AI evolved from early logical programs and the 1956 Dartmouth conference through expert systems to machine learning, deep learning and today’s generative AI.

steps: AI and the Internet of Things (IoT) affect daily life by making services more automated, connected and responsive.
AI can recommend music, videos and products by learning from a person’s choices, and can answer questions through voice assistants.
IoT connects devices such as phones, watches, home appliances, vehicles and sensors to the internet so they can collect and exchange data.
Smart-home devices, such as connected lights, thermostats and security cameras, can be controlled remotely and may save time or energy.
In healthcare, wearable devices can record activity or heart rate, while connected equipment can help health workers monitor patients.
In transport and public services, connected sensors can support traffic management, navigation and monitoring of infrastructure.
These technologies can improve convenience, accessibility, productivity and the speed of some services.
They also create concerns about privacy because devices may collect personal, location or health data, sometimes without users fully understanding how it is used.
Cybersecurity is another concern: insecure devices or networks may be hacked, causing data theft, surveillance or disruption of services.
AI systems may make unfair or incorrect decisions if their data or design is biased, and people may find it difficult to understand or challenge those decisions.
Dependence on connected technology, unequal access to it, job changes and the environmental cost of producing and powering devices are further social concerns.
Using secure devices, collecting only necessary data, explaining how AI decisions are made and providing human oversight can help reduce these risks.
items.finalAnswer: AI and IoT make daily life more convenient through smart services, healthcare and connected devices, but raise concerns about privacy, cybersecurity, bias, unequal access and dependence on technology.

steps: AI can support personalised learning by adjusting lessons and practice to a learner’s progress; for example, a language-learning app can give extra vocabulary exercises when a student struggles.
Intelligent tutoring systems can provide hints and step-by-step practice; for example, a mathematics program can show a hint after a student makes an error instead of only marking the answer wrong.
AI assessment tools can check objective quizzes quickly and give immediate feedback, helping students identify mistakes while they are learning.
Learning analytics can help teachers notice patterns, such as repeated errors or missed assignments, so they can provide timely support to students who may need it.
Speech-recognition tools can help students practise pronunciation by comparing spoken words with the expected pronunciation.
Text-to-speech and speech-to-text tools can support learners with visual, reading or writing difficulties by reading text aloud or converting spoken answers into text.
Translation and language-support tools can help students understand unfamiliar words and learning materials in another language.
AI-powered educational chatbots can answer common questions and guide students to relevant explanations or resources outside classroom hours.
Teachers can use AI tools to prepare quizzes, examples and summaries, saving preparation time and allowing more attention for discussion and individual support.
AI should support, not replace, teachers; teachers need to check the accuracy and suitability of AI-generated content.
Schools should protect students’ personal data, check tools for bias and make sure students have fair access to the technology.
items.finalAnswer: AI enhances education through personalised lessons, tutoring, rapid feedback, learning analytics, accessibility and language tools, while teachers must check accuracy, protect student data and ensure fair access.

steps: AI and IoT can create challenges involving privacy, cybersecurity, safety, discrimination, transparency and responsibility when something goes wrong.
Policy and regulatory frameworks set rules for how these technologies may be designed and used, protect people’s rights and provide ways to investigate or address harm.
Privacy and data-protection rules can require organisations to explain why personal data is collected, use it only for appropriate purposes and protect it from unauthorised access.

The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is an example of a data-protection framework. It gives people rights concerning their personal data and places duties on organisations that process it.
The European Union’s AI Act is a risk-based framework that imposes requirements on certain AI systems, with stricter rules for uses considered higher risk.
Cybersecurity standards and regulations can encourage organisations to assess risks, secure connected devices, update software and report or respond to security incidents.
Governments and organisations may also issue AI ethics guidelines covering fairness, transparency, human oversight and accountability.
These frameworks are effective when their rules are clear, relevant to changing technology and supported by adequate resources for enforcement.
Effectiveness also depends on independent audits, meaningful penalties for violations, reporting channels and access to remedies for affected people.
International cooperation is important because AI services and connected devices often operate across national borders.
Frameworks can be less effective when rules are vague, enforcement is weak, organisations cannot be held accountable or people lack information about their rights.
Regular review and consultation with the public, experts, businesses and affected communities help keep policies practical and up to date.
items.finalAnswer: Policy frameworks such as the GDPR and EU AI Act protect rights and manage AI and IoT risks; their effectiveness depends on clear, current rules, enforcement, audits, remedies and international cooperation.

steps: Algorithmic bias occurs when an AI system produces systematically unfair results for particular people or groups.
Bias may enter through unrepresentative training data, historical inequalities in the data, incorrect labels, choices made during system design or the way results are used.
For example, a hiring system trained on past recruitment records may disadvantage qualified applicants from groups that were under-represented in those records.
In AI-powered decision-making, bias can lead to unfair outcomes in areas such as hiring, lending, education, healthcare and policing.
These outcomes may deny people opportunities or services, reinforce existing discrimination and reduce trust in organisations and AI systems.
A person affected by a decision may also have difficulty challenging it if the system’s reasoning is unclear or there is no human review.
Use diverse, representative and good-quality data, and check it for missing groups and historical unfairness before training the system.
Test the system before and after deployment using appropriate measures to compare errors and outcomes across different groups.
Have independent experts audit high-impact AI systems and document their data, purpose, limitations, tests and changes.
Use explainable systems where possible, tell people when AI affects a decision and provide a clear way to request an explanation or appeal.
Keep a qualified human responsible for reviewing important decisions rather than relying blindly on an automated result.
Monitor deployed systems regularly, correct discovered harms, and involve affected communities in the design and evaluation process.
items.finalAnswer: Algorithmic bias can unfairly deny opportunities, reinforce discrimination and undermine trust; mitigate it with representative data, fairness testing, independent audits, transparency, human review, appeals and ongoing monitoring.

steps: Responsible AI and IoT should respect human rights, dignity, safety and the well-being of people and communities.
Guideline: Identify the intended purpose and possible harms before development, and do not deploy a system if its risks cannot be managed adequately.
Guideline: Collect only the data needed for a clear purpose; obtain appropriate consent, explain data use and provide ways to access, correct or delete data where applicable.
Guideline: Protect information and connected devices with secure design, access controls, encryption where appropriate, software updates and a plan for responding to security incidents.
Guideline: Use relevant and representative data, test for errors and unfair effects on different groups, and correct problems before and after deployment.
Guideline: Tell users when they are interacting with AI or when AI substantially affects a decision; explain important system limitations in understandable language.
Guideline: Keep a responsible human involved in high-impact decisions and provide people with a way to question or appeal decisions.
Guideline: Clearly assign responsibility for system design, operation and harm; keep records of testing, decisions, incidents and changes.
Guideline: Test AI and IoT systems for safety, reliability and accessibility before use, and monitor them regularly after deployment.
Guideline: Design connected products to collect no more data than necessary, use secure default settings and provide a straightforward way to disable unnecessary data collection or connectivity.
Guideline: Consider effects on employment, the environment and people with limited access to technology; make systems as inclusive and energy-conscious as practicable.
Guideline: Review systems when technology, data or circumstances change, and suspend or withdraw a system if serious risks cannot be corrected.
items.finalAnswer: Develop and use AI and IoT safely, fairly and transparently: protect privacy and security, test for harm and bias, keep human oversight and accountability, provide explanations and appeals, and monitor systems throughout their use.
